title: Saving for College with Compound Interest
learningObjectives: Understand how time and compound interest increase savings for post-secondary education and why starting early helps money grow faster
Explain that compound interest means earning interest on the original principal and on accumulated interest, so the balance grows faster over time
Identify that increasing the principal, interest rate, compounding frequency, or saving time makes the final amount larger

explanations.text: Compound interest means you earn interest on both the money you saved and the interest already earned, so your balance grows faster than with simple interest alone.

evidence.quote: Compound interest is when you earn interest on both the money you save and the interest you earn.

explanations.text: Investing $1,000 at 5 percent compounded once a year illustrates compounding: it grows to $1,050 after one year and to $1,102.50 after two years because the second year earns interest on $1,050, not just the original principal.

evidence.quote: So let's say you invest $1,000 (your principal) and it earns 5 percent (interest rate) once a year (the compounding frequency).
After the first year, you would have $1,050—your original principal, plus 5 percent, or $50.

explanations.text: Starting sooner lets money grow faster, and increasing the principal, interest rate, compounding frequency, or the number of years makes savings grow even faster.

evidence.quote: The sooner you start saving in an account that pays interest, the faster your money can grow.
Increasing the compounding frequency or your interest rate or adding to your principal can help your savings grow even faster.
